title: Raft Deep Dive
summary: Raft elects a leader and replicates a log for consensus. Understanding elections, terms, log matching, and commit rules is essential for etcd, Consul, and many coordination services.

sections.title: Roles and terms
paragraphs: Nodes are followers, candidates, or leaders. Terms are monotonically increasing eras. A leader for a term handles client writes and replicates log entries.
Heartbeats reset election timers. If followers time out, they become candidates and request votes. Majority wins; otherwise term increments and retry.

sections.title: Log replication
paragraphs: Clients write to the leader. Entries are appended locally then sent to followers. An entry is committed when stored on a majority; then applied to the state machine.
The log matching property ensures consistency: if two logs have the same index and term, prior entries match. Conflicts are resolved by overwriting follower suffixes.

sections.title: Safety and availability
paragraphs: Raft remains available with majority. A network partition that isolates the leader causes a new election on the majority side; the old leader steps down on seeing a higher term.
Membership changes need careful joint consensus. Mis-managed reconfiguration is a common outage class in real clusters.

sections.title: Using Raft in designs
paragraphs: Put Raft where you need strong leadership and a replicated log: metadata, configuration, small coordination state — not bulk data paths.
etcd uses Raft for Kubernetes state; if you embed Raft, budget for disk fsync latency on the log.

deepDive.title: Raft Deep Dive — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Raft Deep Dive in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Raft Deep Dive — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Raft Deep Dive include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Raft Deep Dive — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Raft Deep Dive intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

practices: Separate bulk data from Raft-managed metadata
pitfalls: Using Raft as a general-purpose database
keyTakeaways: Raft = elected leader + replicated log + majority commit
Safety depends on term and log rules
Use it for coordination, not high-volume data
whyItMatters: Many 'CP' systems you depend on are Raft under the hood. Designing around them requires knowing what the log guarantees — and what it costs.
reflectionQuestions: What state in your design must be under consensus vs eventually consistent storage?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
